messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 22
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Call Center Agent
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 61

She is 22, South Eastern Asian, married, and works as a call center agent, a job that requires her to sound calm and pleasant even when she is tired, upset, or afraid. Before the assault, she describes herself as steady and responsible, the kind of person who keeps going because other people depend on her. She had recently been adjusting to married life while balancing long shifts and the pressure of helping at home, and she remembers feeling proud that she could manage so much at once.

The assault happens after an ordinary day that does not feel like it will become the dividing line in her life. She had not expected danger from the person who harms her, which is part of what makes the event so difficult to place in her mind afterward. In the days that follow, she moves through her routine as if from a distance. She goes to work, answers calls, and repeats the same polite phrases, but inside she feels split open and unreal, as if the life she is living belongs to someone else. She does not talk about what happened at first. She tells herself she can handle it, that she just needs time, and she tries to push the memory away by staying busy.

That effort does not last. Soon, the memory begins returning without permission. Certain sounds, tones of voice, or the feel of being approached too closely can trigger a sudden surge of fear. At work, when a caller becomes loud or aggressive, her body reacts before her mind can catch up: her chest tightens, her hands tremble on the keyboard, and she has to focus hard to keep her voice from shaking. She becomes careful about everything around her, noticing exits, listening for footsteps, and checking locks more than once. Even at home, where she is with her husband and should feel safest, she remains tense. She sits with her back against the wall, startles easily, and has trouble relaxing enough to sleep.

Night becomes its own punishment. She begins to dread bedtime because she knows she may dream about the assault or wake suddenly with her heart racing. On the worst nights, she sleeps only in short stretches, waking sweaty and disoriented, reaching for her phone just to make sure she is still present in her own room. When she does fall asleep, the dreams are vivid and bodily, leaving her shaken for hours afterward. In the morning she often feels exhausted but unable to rest, as though her body has forgotten how to settle. She drinks more tea and coffee than before to make it through work, then finds that the extra caffeine worsens the sense that her nerves are always exposed.

She also notices changes in how she relates to other people. She withdraws from friends and avoids situations that might remind her of the assault. She declines outings, stays quiet in group conversations, and feels irritated when people ask why she seems distant. Shame makes it hard for her to speak openly, even with her husband, and she worries that if she tells the details, she will be seen differently. At times she feels numb rather than sad, as if her emotions have been wrapped in thick cloth. She expects herself to recover quickly and becomes frustrated when she cannot. On some days she blames herself, replaying the event and searching for the moment she thinks she should have done something differently. On other days she feels angry, but the anger has nowhere to go, so it turns inward.

Over time, the world becomes smaller. She plans routes carefully, avoids being alone after dark, and feels uneasy in places where she cannot control who is near her. Even simple tasks can take more effort because she is always braced for something to go wrong. At work she still performs well enough to keep her job, but it costs her more than others can see. She uses breaks to sit quietly and regain her composure, not wanting colleagues to notice when she is close to tears. She presents as composed, yet she lives with a constant sense of threat, as if her body has remained in the moment of the assault even when her life has moved on.

When she speaks about herself now, she does so carefully. She is trying to function, trying to protect her marriage, trying to stay employed, and trying to understand why the fear remains so immediate. Beneath all of that is a deep wish to feel like she belongs to her own life again.
